meta.title: Who originally recorded "Try a Little Tenderness"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Otis Redding. The song was published in London in 1932 and first cut by British dance bands that December — though sources disagree on which band got there first.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'Try a Little Tenderness'?
meta.ogDescription: Otis Redding's 1966 Stax version is definitive, not original. The song dates to November 1932 and was recorded by British dance bands that December.

answer.label: Not an Otis Redding original — the song is a 1932 British dance-band number, cut by the Ray Noble Orchestra with Val Rosing that December
answer.originalArtist: Ray Noble Orchestra (vocal by Val Rosing)
answer.originalArtistDates: Ray Noble, 1903-1978, English bandleader; Val Rosing, 1910-1969, British dance-band vocalist
answer.sourceLine: Otis Redding’s 1966 Volt single is so total a performance that it reads as an origin, but the song was published in London on 4 November 1932, written by Harry M. Woods with Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly. Wikipedia records the first recording as the Ray Noble Orchestra’s session of 8 December 1932, sung by Val Rosing and issued on HMV B-6284 in Britain and Victor 24263 in America. We flag this page as disputed for one reason: a specialist discography of the singer Maurice Elwin dates a Carroll Gibbons and the Savoy Hotel Orpheans recording to 1 December 1932 — a week earlier — and other British bands, Jack Payne among them, were on the song in the same weeks. What is not in doubt is the direction of travel: whoever got to the microphone first, it was a British dance band in 1932, not Otis Redding.

trail: Wikipedia’s article on the song ↗ gives the publication date of 4 November 1932 by Campbell, Connelly & Co., Ltd., and states that it was first recorded on 8 December 1932 by the Ray Noble Orchestra with Val Rosing.
Val Rosing’s own article ↗ repeats the claim independently, describing his vocal on the Ray Noble version as the first recording of the song.

A discography devoted to the British dance-band singer Maurice Elwin dates a Carroll Gibbons and Savoy Hotel Orpheans session ↗ to 1 December 1932 in London, Columbia CB-546 — earlier than Noble’s, which is why this page is marked disputed.
MusicBrainz ↗ carries the Ray Noble recording attached to the February 1933 US release pairing it with Don Bestor’s “Close to Your Heart”.

authors.name: Ray Noble Orchestra (vocal by Val Rosing)
authors.heading: Ray Noble & his Orchestra
authors.metaLine: Ray Noble, 1903-1978 - English bandleader and composer; Val Rosing, 1910-1969, vocalist
authors.bio: Ray Noble was a Brighton-born Royal Academy of Music graduate who led the New Mayfair Dance Orchestra ↗ from 1929 and became one of the defining figures of the British dance-band era before moving to New York in 1934 with Al Bowlly and hiring a young Glenn Miller to assemble his American band. The vocal on the 8 December 1932 session was by Val Rosing ↗, born Valerian Rosing, best known as a singer with Henry Hall’s BBC Dance Orchestra. Rosing later emigrated to America, changed his name to Gilbert Russell and worked as a Hollywood vocal coach. His reading is light, mannered and hopeful — a polite instruction set, not a plea.

authors.name: Otis Redding
authors.heading: Otis Redding
authors.bio: Redding recorded the song at Stax in Memphis in 1966 with Booker T. & the M.G.’s, Isaac Hayes shaping the arrangement, and released it on Volt/Atco V-141 and on Complete & Unbelievable: The Otis Redding Dictionary of Soul. He rebuilt it from the ground up: a slow, almost hymnal opening that escalates into an unstoppable finish. Stax co-founder Jim Stewart called it a performance that summed up who Redding was. It peaked at No. 25 on the Billboard Hot 100, entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2015 and sits at No. 136 on Rolling Stone’s 500 Greatest Songs list. The only error anyone makes about it is chronological.

authors.name: Harry M. Woods, Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly
authors.heading: Woods, Campbell & Connelly
authors.metaLine: Harry M. Woods, 1896-1970, American; Jimmy Campbell, 1903-1967 and Reg Connelly, 1895-1963, English
authors.bio: Harry M. Woods ↗ was a Tin Pan Alley composer whose catalogue includes “When the Red, Red Robin Comes Bob, Bob, Bobbin’ Along” and “Side by Side”; he was born with a deformed left hand and was pushed toward the piano by his mother, a concert singer. Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly ↗ were English songwriters and publishers who had worked together since about 1925 and founded the firm Campbell Connelly in 1929 — the same partnership behind “Show Me the Way to Go Home” and “Goodnight Sweetheart”. Their company published this song on 4 November 1932.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The famous version is a cover of a pre-war British standard. The only genuinely open question is which 1932 dance band recorded it first.

items.who: Otis Redding wrote or originated it
items.why: Redding’s recording is a 1966 Stax reading of a song published in London in November 1932. He did not write it and was not the first to record it.

items.who: Ray Noble Orchestra, vocal by Val Rosing, 8 December 1932
items.why: Wikipedia states this was the first recording, issued on HMV B-6284 and on Victor 24263 in America in February 1933. It is the best-documented early recording.

items.who: Carroll Gibbons and the Savoy Hotel Orpheans, 1 December 1932
items.why: A specialist discography dates a London session with Maurice Elwin and the Carlyle Cousins to 1 December 1932, Columbia CB-546 — a week before Noble’s. It does not itself claim to be the first, and we could not corroborate the date against a second source.

misattribution.truthLine: It is a 1932 British dance-band song. Whether Ray Noble or Carroll Gibbons cut it first is unsettled — but Otis Redding, who was born in 1941, was never in the running.

context.heading: How a 1932 dance-band number became a soul monument
lead: The interesting question is not why people forget the 1932 record — it is why Otis Redding’s version erased not one predecessor but dozens. Between its publication in London in November 1932 and Redding’s Memphis session, the song had been through Ted Lewis, Ruth Etting, Bing Crosby, Frank Sinatra twice, and a whole shelf of British dance bands. It was a well-worn standard, the kind of thing an artist picks up because everybody already knows it.

What Redding and Isaac Hayes did was change the song’s grammar. The 1932 arrangements treat the title as gentle advice, delivered at a tempo you could dance to in a hotel ballroom. The Stax version treats it as something the singer has to survive, starting almost motionless and ending at full sprint, with Booker T. & the M.G.’s pushing the floor out from under it. When a performance reorganises a song that completely, the earlier readings stop sounding like versions of the same thing — which is exactly how an origin gets overwritten.
detailsBody: 4 November 1932 — the song is published in London by Campbell, Connelly & Co., Ltd., music by Harry M. Woods, lyrics by Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly.

1 December 1932 — a specialist discography dates a London session by Carroll Gibbons and the Savoy Hotel Orpheans, vocals by Maurice Elwin and the Carlyle Cousins, issued on Columbia CB-546. This is the disputed earliest claim.

8 December 1932 — the Ray Noble Orchestra records it with Val Rosing on vocal; Wikipedia calls this the first recording. Issued on HMV B-6284 in Britain and, in February 1933, on Victor 24263 in America.
9 January 1933 — Bing Crosby records it for Brunswick.
1933 — Ted Lewis (Columbia 2748 D) and Ruth Etting (Melotone 12625) have hits with it in the United States.
1946 and 1960 — Frank Sinatra records it twice, keeping it in circulation as a ballad standard.

1966 — Otis Redding records it at Stax with Booker T. & the M.G.’s and Isaac Hayes; released on Volt/Atco V-141 and on Complete & Unbelievable: The Otis Redding Dictionary of Soul. It reaches No. 25 on the Billboard Hot 100.
1969 — Three Dog Night’s version reaches No. 29 on the Billboard Hot 100.
context.pull: It was a thirty-four-year-old standard when Stax got hold of it.
